scene.testo: The Hubble Space Telescope has orbited Earth for more than 35 years. It has been repaired five times by astronauts in spacesuits. And no telescope flying today can fully take its place. Here is why it is almost impossible to replace.

Imagine you are floating beside it, 340 miles above Earth, moving at 17,500 mph. It is the size of a school bus. Its mirror is the width of a king bed. And the stars behind it are billions of years old.

So why can't we just build another one? The answer is not money. It is not even technology. It is something far stranger, and it begins with a mistake that nearly destroyed the telescope before it did anything.

Hubble launched on April 24, 1990, aboard the space shuttle Discovery. It was released into orbit about 380 miles up. It weighs roughly 24,500 pounds, about the same as two full-grown elephants plus a few more tons.
It is about 43.5 feet long. That is roughly the length of a large school bus. Its main mirror is 7.9 feet across. NASA built it to look at light that Earth's air blurs, bends, and blocks.

Here is the first secret. Our atmosphere distorts starlight. That is why stars twinkle. A telescope above the air sees sharp, steady images. Hubble sits above all of it, looking at the universe without the blur.

It also sees light our atmosphere blocks completely, like ultraviolet. Hubble can observe in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light. That combination is rare, and each type of light tells scientists something different about a star or galaxy.

But the first images were a disaster. In June 1990, NASA found the main mirror had been ground to the wrong shape. The error was tiny, about one-fiftieth the thickness of a human hair. It was enough to ruin everything.

The pictures were blurry. Newspapers mocked the telescope. Late-night comedians made jokes. A project that cost billions seemed to be a failure. Careful testing later traced the problem to an instrument used while the mirror was being made.

Now comes the part that changes everything. Hubble was designed to be visited. Astronauts could fly up in the shuttle, grab the telescope, and fix it. No other big observatory had ever been built like that.

In December 1993, space shuttle Endeavour carried seven astronauts to Hubble. They worked for five spacewalks over 11 days. Their job was to install new optics, a kind of corrective glasses for a telescope that could not see clearly.

Imagine the pressure. Millions of people watching. A billion-dollar telescope in your gloved hands. Every bolt matters. A dropped tool floats away forever. A tiny slip could damage the only instrument we have.

The fix was called COSTAR. It was installed in a space the size of a phone booth, and it worked like glasses for the instruments. When the new images came back in January 1994, they were sharp. The mission was a triumph.

And that was only the first visit. Shuttle crews returned in 1997, 1999, 2002, and 2009. Five servicing missions in total. Each one upgraded the telescope with new instruments, new gyroscopes, new batteries, and new computers.

Think about what that means. Hubble is not the telescope that was launched in 1990. Almost every key instrument has been swapped out over the years. It is more like a ship rebuilt plank by plank by its crews.

The shuttle was essential. It could carry astronauts, parts, and a robotic arm to a telescope in orbit. It could hold the telescope steady while crews worked. No spacecraft flying today can do all of that.

The space shuttle fleet retired in July 2011. That is the second secret. The only vehicle that ever repaired Hubble is a museum piece now. No astronaut has touched the telescope since the final visit in May 2009.

That last visit was STS-125, flown by shuttle Atlantis. Seven astronauts. Five spacewalks again. They installed a new camera and a new spectrograph, and they repaired two instruments that had stopped working, in ways never planned on the ground.
Why does that matter? Because a replacement would need a way to be serviced too. And right now, no operating spacecraft can reach Hubble, hold it, and let humans work on it the way the shuttle did.

Now, you might say, build a bigger one. NASA did build another giant. The James Webb Space Telescope launched on December 25, 2021. Its mirror is 21.3 feet across, much larger than Hubble's. So it should replace Hubble. Right?

Wrong. Webb is built for a different job. It looks mainly at infrared light, which shows the coldest, oldest, most distant objects. Hubble sees mostly visible and ultraviolet light. They are partners, not twins.

Webb also lives far away. It sits about 1,000,000 miles from Earth, four times farther than the Moon. Hubble is only about 340 miles up. That distance is why astronauts could reach Hubble but cannot reach Webb.

Webb must stay extremely cold to see infrared, so its sunshield is the size of a tennis court. It works in deep cold, around minus 370 degrees Fahrenheit on its coldest side. Hubble sits in warmer, closer, easier territory.

And here is the key difference. Nobody can fix Webb if something breaks. It was designed without servicing in mind. Hubble's strength is that humans improved it again and again. That is the thing nobody has been able to copy.

Now think about what Hubble has actually seen. In 1995, it stared at a tiny empty-looking patch of sky for about 10 days. The result, called the Hubble Deep Field, revealed thousands of galaxies in a spot the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length.

It changed how we think about the universe. Hubble has helped measure how fast the universe is expanding. It has helped scientists estimate the age of the universe at roughly 13.8 billion years. These are documented results, repeated by many teams.

In 1998, observations including Hubble's helped reveal that the expansion of the universe is speeding up. The cause is called dark energy. Scientists still do not know exactly what it is. The 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics honored that discovery.

Hubble also watched a comet crash into a planet. In July 1994, pieces of comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 slammed into Jupiter, one after another. Hubble captured dark scars in the clouds, some of them larger than Earth.

It has photographed Pluto's moons, storms on Saturn, and auroras on Jupiter. It has watched stars being born inside the Pillars of Creation, towers of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula, about 6,500 light years away.

Here is the surprise. After more than 35 years, Hubble still produces new science every day. Thousands of scientific papers use its data every year. That long record lets researchers compare the same objects across decades, like frames in a very slow movie.

That is something a new telescope cannot buy. A telescope launched tomorrow starts its record at zero. Hubble has a library of observations stretching back to 1990. Time itself is part of what makes it so valuable.

But Hubble is aging. Imagine it as a very old car that is still winning races. Its gyroscopes, the spinning devices that point it, wear out. In 2024, one gyroscope began giving faulty readings, and NASA switched Hubble to a mode using just one.

With one gyroscope, Hubble turns more slowly and can see a bit less of the sky at any moment. NASA said the telescope keeps doing strong science. It simply has less flexibility. Engineers keep watching the remaining parts very closely.

Now the other problem. Hubble is slowly sinking. At about 340 miles up, there is still a thin trace of air. It drags on the telescope. Over the years, the orbit decays, and sooner or later Hubble will fall back toward Earth.

NASA estimates that, without a boost, Hubble has a significant chance of reentering the atmosphere in the mid-2030s. The exact date depends on how active the Sun is, because solar activity puffs up the upper air and increases drag.

So could someone give it a lift? In 2022, NASA studied a proposal with a private company to launch a mission that would dock with Hubble and raise its orbit. Studies were completed. But no such mission has flown, and NASA has said the risk was significant.

Docking is hard because Hubble was never built for it. The shuttle grabbed it with the robotic arm. Hubble does carry a special grapple fixture and a soft-capture mechanism, added in 2009 so a future spacecraft could catch it. A small gift from the last crew.

Imagine how delicate that would be. Two spacecraft, each moving 17,500 mph, must meet and touch gently. If the visitor bumps Hubble too hard, or damages a solar panel, the world's most famous telescope could be lost.

What about a brand-new Hubble? NASA studied future large telescopes. One concept, the Habitable Worlds Observatory, is aimed at finding Earth-like planets. It is still in early planning. A telescope like that takes decades and billions of dollars.

Hubble's own cost tells the story. NASA's figures put the total cost of Hubble, including servicing missions, well over 10 billion dollars across its lifetime. And that is only the money. The shuttle missions also carried real risk to human lives.

Also, building a telescope takes patience. Webb was first proposed in the 1990s and launched in 2021. That is about 25 years. Telescopes are rarely replaced quickly, because every mirror and instrument is nearly one of a kind.

Hubble's mirror is also special. It was polished so smooth that, if it were scaled up to the size of the United States, its biggest bump would be only a few inches tall. That level of smoothness is hard to repeat.

Even the ground matters. Big telescopes on mountains now use adaptive optics to cancel atmospheric blur, and some produce very sharp images. But they still cannot see ultraviolet light from the surface, and clouds, weather, and daylight still limit them.

So here is the real answer. Hubble is almost impossible to replace because of four things together. It sees ultraviolet and visible light from above the air. It has 35 years of records. It was rebuilt by humans. And no servicing ship exists today.

Picture the final moment. One day, years from now, Hubble will finish its work. NASA has said it plans to bring it down safely, with a controlled reentry, so no large pieces fall on populated areas. That is the responsible ending.

And here is the most surprising detail. When astronauts left Hubble for the last time in May 2009, they added a final gift: a docking ring for a future visitor. It has waited, silent, ever since. A door left open for a guest who may never arrive.

Why is the Hubble Space Telescope almost impossible to replace? In this Orbital Days documentary, we follow the telescope from its 1990 launch and the blurry mirror mistake to five daring shuttle servicing missions, and explain how it differs from the James Webb Space Telescope.
